title: Benchmark parallel vs sequential for a list of 10 elements vs 10 million elements and explain the overhead.
shortTitle: Benchmark parallel vs sequential for 10 elements vs 10 million and explain the overhead
keyPoints: For 10 elements, parallel is slower because the fixed split/merge overhead dominates the trivial work
For 10 million elements, parallel is faster because the work dwarfs the overhead across multiple cores
The crossover point depends on per-element cost, core count, and source splittability
A proper micro-benchmark uses JMH to account for JIT warm-up and dead-code elimination
Hand-rolled nanoTime benchmarks are indicative but not reliable for production decisions
The lesson is to measure rather than assume: default to sequential and parallelize only after measuring

s1_definition.oneliner: Parallel loses on tiny inputs where overhead dominates and wins on huge inputs where work dominates the fixed cost.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Small data (10 elements)**: parallel is slower because splitting, scheduling, and merging cost more than the work itself.
- **Large data (10M elements)**: parallel wins because the work across cores far exceeds the overhead.
- **Crossover point** depends on per-element cost, core count, and source splittability.
- **JMH** is the proper tool for reliable micro-benchmarking; `nanoTime` is indicative only.
- **Default to sequential** and parallelize only after measuring with representative data.
s1_definition.analogy: Hiring extra clerks at National Bank of India to total a three-line ledger wastes time coordinating them. But for a million-line ledger, the extra clerks finish far sooner because the work outweighs the coordination.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To decide whether parallelism pays off, you benchmark a sequential sum against a parallel sum on both a tiny list and a huge list. For 10 elements, the parallel version is much slower because the fixed cost of splitting, scheduling, and merging dwarfs the actual work. For 10 million elements, the parallel version is several times faster because spreading the work across cores saves far more time than the overhead costs.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh uses this comparison to decide whether to parallelize the nightly salary-sum job. He uses JMH for reliable numbers because hand-rolled `nanoTime` benchmarks suffer from JIT warm-up, dead-code elimination, and GC pauses that distort results.

The lesson is that parallelism is never free. The crossover point depends on per-element cost, core count, and source splittability. For cheap operations like addition, the crossover is around 100K+ elements. For expensive operations, it can be much lower. A senior engineer defaults to sequential and parallelizes only after measuring with representative data.

Remember one sentence: measure, do not guess: parallel wins on large data with expensive work, but loses on small data where overhead dominates.
